questions.question: What is the magnitude of $2\underset{\sim}{u}+3\underset{\sim}{v}$?
questions.answer: $|2\mathbf u+3\mathbf v|^2=4|\mathbf u|^2+12\,\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+9|\mathbf v|^2$. This depends on $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$, which are not given, so the magnitude cannot be determined (D).

questions.question: The polynomial $P(x)=x^3+5x^2+bx+c$ has a double root at $x=-1$. What are the values of $b$ and $c$?
What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(4\cos^2x-5\right)dx$?
questions.answer: $4\cos^2x-5=2(1+\cos2x)-5=2\cos2x-3$. $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}(2\cos2x-3)dx=\Big[\sin2x-3x\Big]_0^{\pi/4}=1-\dfrac{3\pi}4$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following is equivalent to $\left|\operatorname{proj}_{\underset{\sim}{v}}\underset{\sim}{u}\right|$?
questions.answer: $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=\dfrac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|^2}\mathbf v$, so its magnitude is $\dfrac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|}{|\mathbf v|^2}|\mathbf v|=\dfrac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|}{|\mathbf v|}$ (C). The absolute value is needed since the magnitude is never negative (B can be negative).

questions.question: Which of the following gives the same curve as $x=\sin t$ and $y=-t$, for all real numbers $t$?
questions.answer: The original curve is $x=\sin(-y)=-\sin y$. A: $x=\sin y$, which is a different curve. C and D: $y=t^2+\pi$ or $y=-t^2$ cannot take all real values, so they give only part of the curve. B: $y=2t+\pi$ takes all real values and $x=-\sin(2t+\pi)=-\sin y$, which is the same curve (B).

questions.question: How many seven letter words can be formed from the word THUNDER, such that T and R must be at either end, and U is somewhere to the right of D?
questions.answer: T and R occupy the two ends in $2!=2$ ways. The other five letters fill the middle, and U is to the right of D in exactly half of the $5!$ arrangements, i.e. $\dfrac{5!}{2}=60$. Total $=2\times60=120$ (B).

questions.question: What is the number of solutions to the equation $x+e^{-x}=\big||x|-2\big|$?
questions.answer: Sketch $y=x+e^{-x}$ and $y=\big||x|-2\big|$ (a W shape with minima at $x=\pm2$ and a local maximum of 2 at $x=0$). For large positive $x$, $e^{-x}\to0$ so the exponential curve approaches $y=x$, which lies above the right arm $y=x-2$ and so never meets it. The curve $y=x+e^{-x}$ has a minimum value of 1 at $x=0$ and crosses the middle part of the W (the peak region near $x=0$) twice, once either side of the $y$-axis. There are no other intersections, so there are 2 solutions (C).

questions.question: The gradient of the normal at any point $P$ on a particular curve is half the gradient of the line joining $P$ and the origin. Which of the following differential equations does this curve satisfy?
questions.answer: Normal gradient $=-\dfrac1{dy/dx}$ and the gradient of $OP$ is $\dfrac yx$. So $-\dfrac1{dy/dx}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac yx$. Taking reciprocals, $-\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2x}y$, i.e. $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2x}y=0$ (C).

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\sin(2x)-\sqrt3\cos(2x)$. What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{f(x)}2\right)dx$?
questions.answer: $f(x)=2\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)$, so the integrand is $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right)$. Let $u=2x-\dfrac\pi3$, $du=2dx$; the limits become $-\dfrac\pi3$ to $\dfrac{2\pi}3$: $I=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\sin^{-1}(\sin u)\,du$. The graph of $\sin^{-1}(\sin u)$ equals $u$ for $|u|\le\dfrac\pi2$ and $\pi-u$ for $\dfrac\pi2\le u\le\dfrac{3\pi}2$. The integral is the signed area: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/2}u\,du=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{\pi^2}4-\dfrac{\pi^2}9\right)=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{72}$ and $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}(\pi-u)du=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)^2-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac\pi3\right)^2=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{72}$. Total $=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{36}$, so $I=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{5\pi^2}{36}=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{72}$ (D).

questions.question: Distinct factors of $337\,500$ are randomly selected. What is the minimum number of distinct factors of $337\,500$ that must be selected to guarantee that the product of these selected factors will be a multiple of $337\,500$?
questions.answer: $337\,500=2^2\times3^3\times5^5$. The product is a multiple of $337\,500$ only if the exponents of 2, 3 and 5 in the product sum to at least 2, 3 and 5 respectively. Worst case: select all factors with no factor of 2, i.e. $3^a5^b$ with $0\le a\le3$, $0\le b\le5$, which is $4\times6=24$ factors. Their product contains no 2. Adding one more factor (which must contain at least one 2, e.g. $2^1$) gives only $2^1$, still not enough (25 factors). A 26th factor adds at least another 2, so the power of 2 is at least $2^2$, and since all 24 factors without 2 are included, the powers of 3 and 5 are far more than needed. So 26 factors are needed (B). (Leaving out all factors with no 3 or no 5 gives smaller worst-case sets of 18 and 12 factors respectively.)

questions.question: Differentiate $(\tan^{-1}x)^2$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac d{dx}(\tan^{-1}x)^2=2\tan^{-1}x\cdot\dfrac1{1+x^2}=\dfrac{2\tan^{-1}x}{1+x^2}$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $u=x+2$ to find $\displaystyle\int(x-1)\sqrt{x+2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $x=u-2$ and $du=dx$. $\displaystyle\int(u-3)u^{1/2}du=\int\left(u^{3/2}-3u^{1/2}\right)du=\dfrac25u^{5/2}-2u^{3/2}+C=\dfrac25(x+2)^{5/2}-2(x+2)^{3/2}+C$.

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac x{1-x^2}<0$.
questions.answer: Multiply both sides by $(1-x^2)^2>0$ (valid for $x\ne\pm1$): $x(1-x^2)<0$, i.e. $x(1-x)(1+x)<0$. The cubic has negative leading coefficient and zeroes at $-1,0,1$, so it is negative for $-1<x<0$ and $x>1$. These avoid $x=\pm1$ (undefined) and $x=0$ (equals 0). Solution: $-1<x<0$ or $x>1$.

questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x-2}{x-5}$. State the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.answer: The range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$: all real $x$ with $x\ne5$.

questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x-2}{x-5}$. Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.answer: Swap $x$ and $y$: $x=\dfrac{y-2}{y-5}$. Then $xy-5x=y-2$, so $y(x-1)=5x-2$ and $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{5x-2}{x-1}$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int3\cos(2x)\cos\left(5x-\dfrac\pi3\right)dx$.
questions.answer: Using $\cos A\cos B=\dfrac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]$ with $A=2x$, $B=5x-\dfrac\pi3$: $\cos2x\cos\left(5x-\dfrac\pi3\right)=\dfrac12\left[\cos\left(3x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\cos\left(7x-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right]$ (cosine is even). So $\displaystyle\int=\dfrac32\left[\dfrac13\sin\left(3x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\dfrac17\sin\left(7x-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right]+C=\dfrac12\sin\left(3x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\dfrac3{14}\sin\left(7x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+C$.

questions.question: Solve $2\operatorname{cosec}\theta-4\cot\theta=3$ using the $t$-formula, for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. Give your answer(s) correct to 3 significant figures.
questions.answer: Let $t=\tan\dfrac\theta2$: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}$, so $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1+t^2}{2t}$ and $\cot\theta=\dfrac{1-t^2}{2t}$. Then $\dfrac{2(1+t^2)-4(1-t^2)}{2t}=3$, so $6t^2-2=6t$, i.e. $3t^2-3t-1=0$ and $t=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{21}}6$. $\dfrac\theta2=\arctan\dfrac{3+\sqrt{21}}6$ gives $\theta=1.80$; $\dfrac\theta2=\pi+\arctan\dfrac{3-\sqrt{21}}6$ (the principal value is negative, so add $\pi$) gives $\theta=5.77$. Both lie in $[0,2\pi]$. Also $\theta=\pi$ ($t$ undefined) is not a solution since $\cot\pi$ is undefined. $\theta=1.80,\ 5.77$.

questions.question: The region enclosed by $y=e^{-x}$, $y=x$, $x=1$ and $x=3$ is rotated about the $x$-axis. Calculate the volume of the solid of revolution. Give your answer in fully simplified exact form.
questions.answer: On $[1,3]$, $x\ge1>e^{-x}$, so $y=x$ is on top. $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^3\left(x^2-e^{-2x}\right)dx=\pi\left[\dfrac{x^3}3+\dfrac12e^{-2x}\right]_1^3=\pi\left[\left(9+\dfrac12e^{-6}\right)-\left(\dfrac13+\dfrac12e^{-2}\right)\right]=\pi\left(\dfrac{26}3+\dfrac12e^{-6}-\dfrac12e^{-2}\right)$ cubic units.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\mathbf i+\lambda^2\mathbf j$, where $\lambda$ is a real number. Determine the values of $\lambda$ such that $\underset{\sim}{u}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}$ are perpendicular.
questions.answer: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=-6+5\lambda^2=0$, so $\lambda^2=\dfrac65$ and $\lambda=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac65}$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\mathbf i+\lambda^2\mathbf j$, where $\lambda$ is a real number. Explain why $\underset{\sim}{u}$ cannot be parallel to $\underset{\sim}{v}$. (Justify your answer mathematically.)
questions.answer: If parallel, there is a real $r$ with $\mathbf u=r\mathbf v$: $2=-3r$ and $5=r\lambda^2$. The first gives $r=-\dfrac23$, so $\lambda^2=5\div\left(-\dfrac23\right)=-7.5$, which is impossible for real $\lambda$. Hence $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are never parallel. (Alternatively, $\mathbf u$ points into the first quadrant while $\mathbf v$ has negative $x$-component and non-negative $y$-component, so they cannot be scalar multiples.)

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\mathbf i+\lambda^2\mathbf j$. If $\lambda=1$, determine $\underset{\sim}{q}$ such that $\underset{\sim}{u}=\operatorname{proj}_{\underset{\sim}{v}}(\underset{\sim}{u})+\underset{\sim}{q}$.
questions.answer: With $\lambda=1$, $\mathbf v=(-3,1)$. $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=-6+5=-1$ and $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v=10$. $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=\dfrac{-1}{10}(-3,1)=(0.3,-0.1)$. $\mathbf q=\mathbf u-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=(2-0.3,\ 5+0.1)=\begin{pmatrix}1.7\\5.1\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: The roots of $P(x)=8x^3-5x^2+2x-1$ are $\alpha,\beta$ and $\gamma$. Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.
questions.answer: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\dfrac58$ and $\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma=\dfrac28=\dfrac14$. $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)=\dfrac{25}{64}-\dfrac12=-\dfrac7{64}$. (This is negative, so $P$ has non-real roots.)

questions.question: The triangle $ABC$ is right angled at $A$. Let $AB=5$ cm and $\angle ABC=\theta$ radians. If $\theta$ is increasing at a constant rate of $0.1$ radians per second, find the rate at which the perimeter of the triangle is increasing when $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$ radians. Leave your answer in exact form.
questions.answer: $AC=5\tan\theta$ and $BC=\dfrac5{\cos\theta}=5\sec\theta$. Perimeter $p=5+5\tan\theta+5\sec\theta$. $\dfrac{dp}{d\theta}=5\sec^2\theta+5\sec\theta\tan\theta$. $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=\dfrac{dp}{d\theta}\cdot\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=0.1\left(5\sec^2\theta+5\sec\theta\tan\theta\right)$. At $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$: $\sec=2$, $\tan=\sqrt3$, so $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=0.1(20+10\sqrt3)=2+\sqrt3$ cm/s.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction that, for all integers $n\ge1$, $2\times1!+5\times2!+10\times3!+\cdots+(n^2+1)\times n!=n\times(n+1)!$.
questions.answer:
$n=1$: LHS $=(1+1)\times1!=2$, RHS $=1\times2!=2$. True.

Assume true for $n=k$: $2\times1!+\cdots+(k^2+1)k!=k(k+1)!$.

For $n=k+1$: LHS $=k(k+1)!+\left[(k+1)^2+1\right](k+1)!=(k+1)!\left[k+k^2+2k+2\right]=(k+1)!\left(k^2+3k+2\right)=(k+1)!(k+1)(k+2)=(k+1)(k+2)!$, which is RHS for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all $n\ge1$.

questions.question: Show that $\dfrac1{2000}\left(\dfrac1S+\dfrac1{2000-S}\right)=\dfrac1{S(2000-S)}$.

The rate of spread of a flu is modelled by $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S(2000-S)}{5000}$, where $S$ is the total number of people infected after $t$ days. Solve the differential equation using separation of variables to show that $S=\dfrac{2000}{1+Qe^{-0.4t}}$, where $Q$ is a constant.
questions.answer: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dS}{S(2000-S)}=\int\dfrac{dt}{5000}$. By part (i), $\dfrac1{2000}\int\left(\dfrac1S+\dfrac1{2000-S}\right)dS=\dfrac t{5000}+C$, so $\ln\left|\dfrac S{2000-S}\right|=0.4t+C_1$ (multiplying by 2000). Hence $\dfrac S{2000-S}=Ae^{0.4t}$ ($A=\pm e^{C_1}$). $S=Ae^{0.4t}(2000-S)$, so $S\left(1+Ae^{0.4t}\right)=2000Ae^{0.4t}$ and $S=\dfrac{2000Ae^{0.4t}}{1+Ae^{0.4t}}=\dfrac{2000}{1+\frac1Ae^{-0.4t}}$. With $Q=\dfrac1A$: $S=\dfrac{2000}{1+Qe^{-0.4t}}$.

questions.question: The slope field of $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S(2000-S)}{5000}$ is shown, with three regions labelled A (above $S=2000$), B (between $S=0$ and $S=2000$) and C (below $S=0$). Consider the particular solution $S=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}$. In which one of these three regions will the curve of the particular solution lie? You must justify your answer.
questions.answer: For $t\ge0$, $199e^{-0.4t}>0$, so $1+199e^{-0.4t}>1$ and $0<S<2000$. At $t=0$, $S=\dfrac{2000}{200}=10$ and as $t\to\infty$, $S\to2000$ from below. So the curve lies entirely in region B.

questions.question: According to this model, and using $Q=199$, after how many days does the rate of spread reach its maximum? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

questions.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\underset{\sim}{c}$. Show that $\overrightarrow{BN}=\dfrac12\underset{\sim}{c}-\underset{\sim}{b}$, and write a similar expression for $\overrightarrow{CM}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{BN}=\overrightarrow{BA}+\overrightarrow{AN}=-\mathbf b+\dfrac12\mathbf c=\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{CM}=\overrightarrow{CA}+\overrightarrow{AM}=-\mathbf c+\dfrac12\mathbf b=\dfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf c$.

questions.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\underset{\sim}{c}$. Hence, using vectors, show that if $BN$ and $CM$ are perpendicular, then $|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2=5|\mathbf a|^2$, where $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{BC}$.
questions.answer: Perpendicular: $\overrightarrow{BN}\cdot\overrightarrow{CM}=0$. $\left(\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b\right)\cdot\left(\dfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf c\right)=\dfrac14\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c-\dfrac12|\mathbf c|^2-\dfrac12|\mathbf b|^2+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac54\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c-\dfrac12\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)=0$, so $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac25\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)$ (1). Now $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf b$, so $|\mathbf a|^2=|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2-2\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c$. Substituting (1): $|\mathbf a|^2=\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)\left(1-\dfrac45\right)=\dfrac15\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)$. Hence $|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2=5|\mathbf a|^2$.

prev.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\underset{\sim}{c}$. Show that $\overrightarrow{BN}=\dfrac12\underset{\sim}{c}-\underset{\sim}{b}$, and write a similar expression for $\overrightarrow{CM}$.
prev.answer: $\overrightarrow{BN}=\overrightarrow{BA}+\overrightarrow{AN}=-\mathbf b+\dfrac12\mathbf c=\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{CM}=\overrightarrow{CA}+\overrightarrow{AM}=-\mathbf c+\dfrac12\mathbf b=\dfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf c$.

questions.question: The position vectors of particles $P$ and $Q$ at time $t$ minutes are $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\\sin t\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}\cos3t\\\sin3t\end{pmatrix}$ respectively, where $0\le t\le2\pi$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ at time $t$, where $O$ is the origin. Show that $\cos\theta=\cos2t$.
questions.answer: $|\overrightarrow{OP}|=|\overrightarrow{OQ}|=1$, so $\cos\theta=\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\overrightarrow{OQ}=\cos t\cos3t+\sin t\sin3t=\cos(3t-t)=\cos2t$.

questions.question: The position vectors of particles $P$ and $Q$ at time $t$ minutes are $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\\sin t\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}\cos3t\\\sin3t\end{pmatrix}$ respectively, where $0\le t\le2\pi$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ at time $t$, where $O$ is the origin. Find the total time for which $\theta\ge\dfrac\pi4$.
questions.answer: $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and $\cos$ is decreasing on this interval, so $\theta\ge\dfrac\pi4\iff\cos\theta\le\dfrac1{\sqrt2}\iff\cos2t\le\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$. For $0\le2t\le4\pi$ this holds for $2t\in\left[\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{7\pi}4\right]\cup\left[\dfrac{9\pi}4,\dfrac{15\pi}4\right]$, i.e. $t\in\left[\dfrac\pi8,\dfrac{7\pi}8\right]\cup\left[\dfrac{9\pi}8,\dfrac{15\pi}8\right]$. Each interval has length $\dfrac{3\pi}4$, so the total time is $\dfrac{3\pi}2$ minutes.

prev.question: The position vectors of particles $P$ and $Q$ at time $t$ minutes are $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\\sin t\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}\cos3t\\\sin3t\end{pmatrix}$ respectively, where $0\le t\le2\pi$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ at time $t$, where $O$ is the origin. Show that $\cos\theta=\cos2t$.
prev.answer: $|\overrightarrow{OP}|=|\overrightarrow{OQ}|=1$, so $\cos\theta=\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\overrightarrow{OQ}=\cos t\cos3t+\sin t\sin3t=\cos(3t-t)=\cos2t$.

questions.question: A particle is projected from the origin $O$ with initial speed $U$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. The position vector at time $t$ after projection, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Ut\cos\alpha\\Ut\sin\alpha-\dfrac{gt^2}2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) Prove that if the particle passes through the point $P(a,b)$, where $a>0$, then the minimum possible value of $U$ is $\sqrt{g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)}$.
questions.answer:
Eliminate $t=\dfrac x{U\cos\alpha}$: $y=x\tan\alpha-\dfrac{gx^2}{2U^2}\sec^2\alpha=x\tan\alpha-\dfrac{gx^2}{2U^2}\left(1+\tan^2\alpha\right)$. Passing through $(a,b)$ with $T=\tan\alpha$: $b=aT-\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}(1+T^2)$, so $\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}T^2-aT+\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)=0$.

For a real $\alpha$ to exist the discriminant must be non-negative: $a^2-4\cdot\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)\ge0$. Dividing by $a^2$: $1\ge\dfrac{2g}{U^2}\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)$, so $U^2\ge2gb+\dfrac{g^2a^2}{U^2}$, i.e. $U^4-2gbU^2-g^2a^2\ge0$. Complete the square: $(U^2-gb)^2\ge g^2b^2+g^2a^2$, so $|U^2-gb|\ge g\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Since $U^2-gb\le-g\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ would give $U^2\le g(b-\sqrt{a^2+b^2})\le0$, which is impossible, we need $U^2\ge g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)$. The minimum possible value of $U$ is $\sqrt{g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)}$.

questions.question: A particle is projected from the origin $O$ with initial speed $U$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. The position vector at time $t$ after projection, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Ut\cos\alpha\\Ut\sin\alpha-\dfrac{gt^2}2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) Suppose the particle is projected with the minimum possible speed in order to pass through $P(a,b)$. Show that $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}a$.
questions.answer: At the minimum speed the discriminant is zero, so the quadratic $\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}T^2-aT+\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)=0$ has the repeated root $T=\dfrac{a}{2\cdot\frac{ga^2}{2U^2}}=\dfrac{U^2}{ga}$. With $U^2=g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)$: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}a$.

questions.question: A particle is projected from the origin $O$ with initial speed $U$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. The position vector at time $t$ after projection, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Ut\cos\alpha\\Ut\sin\alpha-\dfrac{gt^2}2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) The particle is projected with the minimum possible speed to pass through $P(a,b)$. Deduce that $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)$ bisects the angle between $OP$ and the positive $y$-axis, where $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)$ is the initial velocity vector of the particle.
questions.answer:
Let $\beta$ be the angle $OP$ makes with the positive $x$-axis, so $\tan\beta=\dfrac ba$. The initial velocity makes angle $\alpha$ with the $x$-axis. The angle between $\mathbf v(0)$ and the positive $y$-axis is $\dfrac\pi2-\alpha$ and the angle between $OP$ and $\mathbf v(0)$ is $\alpha-\beta$. To show: $\dfrac\pi2-\alpha=\alpha-\beta$ (this requires $\alpha>\beta$, which holds since $\tan\alpha>\dfrac ba$).

$\tan\left(\dfrac\pi2-\alpha\right)=\cot\alpha=\dfrac a{b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$. Let $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. $\tan(\alpha-\beta)=\dfrac{\tan\alpha-\tan\beta}{1+\tan\alpha\tan\beta}=\dfrac{\frac{b+r}a-\frac ba}{1+\frac{b(b+r)}{a^2}}=\dfrac{r/a}{\frac{a^2+b^2+br}{a^2}}=\dfrac{ar}{r^2+br}=\dfrac a{r+b}$. The two tangents are equal and both angles lie in $\left(0,\dfrac\pi2\right)$, so $\dfrac\pi2-\alpha=\alpha-\beta$: $\mathbf v(0)$ bisects the angle between $OP$ and the positive $y$-axis.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$. What is the value of $|\underset{\sim}{a}|$?
If $f(x)=\sin^{-1}(x-1)$, which of the following is the range of $f(x)$?
questions.answer: The inverse sine function takes principal values only, so its range is $\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]$. The substitution $x\mapsto x-1$ shifts the domain (to $[0,2]$) but does not change the range (B).

questions.question: Which of the following vectors is perpendicular to $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$?
questions.answer: Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product: $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}=6-6=0$ (C).

questions.question: A headmaster realises that there is at least one month of the year when at least 34 pupils have a birthday. What is the minimum possible number of pupils at the school?
questions.answer: If every month had at most 33 birthdays there would be at most $12\times33=396$ pupils. So with 397 pupils (pigeonhole principle) at least one month has at least 34. The minimum is 397 (B).

questions.question: A particle moves so that $x=\tan t$ and $y=x^2$. Which of the following is equal to $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$?
questions.answer: $y=\tan^2t$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2\tan t\sec^2t$ (C).

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. The projection of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ onto $\underset{\sim}{b}$ is $\lambda\underset{\sim}{b}$. What is the value of $\lambda$?
questions.answer: $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf b}\mathbf a=\dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf b|^2}\mathbf b$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{2+2}{1+4}=\dfrac45$ (C).

questions.question: The graphs of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are shown. Which transformation maps $f(x)$ to $g(x)$?
questions.answer: $g$ is symmetric in the $y$-axis, so the right-hand part of $f$ is reflected in the $y$-axis ($f(|x|)$). The result has parts below the $x$-axis, and $g$ has none, so these are reflected above the axis too: $g(x)=|f(|x|)|$ (D).

questions.question: Which of the following slope fields corresponds to the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y-x}x$? (Slope fields A, B, C, D are shown in order.)
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac yx-1$. Horizontal line elements occur along $y=x$. The equation is undefined at $x=0$, so there are no line elements on the $y$-axis. Along $y=0$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-1$. The gradient changes sign on either side of $y=x$. Only slope field D has all these features (D).

questions.question: The nine members of the Fellowship of the Ring are seated randomly around a circular table. What is the probability that the two youngest members of the Fellowship are seated next to each other?
questions.answer: Total circular arrangements of 9 people: $8!$. Treat the two youngest as one block: 8 objects in a circle give $7!$ arrangements, and the block can be ordered internally in $2!$ ways. Probability $=\dfrac{7!\,2!}{8!}$ (D).

questions.question: Let $g(x)=\sin^2x-\dfrac x3$. How many times does the graph of $y=g(x)$ intersect the $x$-axis?
questions.answer: Solve $\sin^2x=\dfrac x3$. Since $0\le\sin^2x\le1$, solutions satisfy $0\le x\le3$. $x=0$ is a solution. $g(1)=\sin^21-\dfrac13>0$ while $g\left(\dfrac14\right)=\sin^2\dfrac14-\dfrac1{12}<0$, so there is a root in $\left(\dfrac14,1\right)$. $g\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)=1-\dfrac\pi6>0$ and $g(\pi)=-\dfrac\pi3<0$, so there is a root in $\left(\dfrac\pi2,\pi\right)$. Graphically, $y=\sin^2x$ meets the line $y=\dfrac x3$ three times in all (C).

questions.question: How many four-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 without repetition?
questions.answer: ${}^7P_4=7\times6\times5\times4=840$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac2{1+x^2}dx$.
questions.answer: $2\Big[\tan^{-1}x\Big]_0^1=2\left(\dfrac\pi4-0\right)=\dfrac\pi2$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac\theta2$ to solve $2\sin\theta+\cos\theta=2$, for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
questions.answer: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$. $\dfrac{4t+1-t^2}{1+t^2}=2$, so $1+4t-t^2=2+2t^2$, i.e. $3t^2-4t+1=0$ and $(3t-1)(t-1)=0$. $t=\dfrac13$ or $t=1$. $\dfrac\theta2=\tan^{-1}\dfrac13$ or $\dfrac\pi4$, so $\theta=2\tan^{-1}\dfrac13\ (\approx0.644)$ or $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$. (Check: $\theta=\pi$, where $t$ is undefined, gives $-1\ne2$, so it is not a solution.)

questions.question: The curve $C$ is defined parametrically by $x=t^2+1$ and $y=t^3-3t$. Find the gradient of the tangent to $C$ when $t=2$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2t$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=3t^2-3$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3t^2-3}{2t}$. At $t=2$: $\dfrac{12-3}4=\dfrac94$.

questions.question: The area, $A$, of a square is increasing at a rate of $12\ \text{cm}^2\text{s}^{-1}$. Find the rate at which the side length, $x$, is increasing when the side length is 3 cm.
questions.answer: $A=x^2$, so $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=2x\dfrac{dx}{dt}$. $12=2(3)\dfrac{dx}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2$ cm/s.

questions.question: Express $\cos2x+\sin2x$ in the form $R\cos(2x-\alpha)$, where $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$.
questions.answer: $R\cos(2x-\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\cos2x+R\sin\alpha\sin2x$, so $R\cos\alpha=1$ and $R\sin\alpha=1$. $R=\sqrt2$ and $\tan\alpha=1$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi4$. $\cos2x+\sin2x=\sqrt2\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)$.

questions.question: Hence solve $\cos2x+\sin2x=1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
questions.answer: $\sqrt2\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)=1$, so $\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$ with $-\dfrac\pi4\le2x-\dfrac\pi4\le\dfrac{15\pi}4$. So $2x-\dfrac\pi4=-\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{7\pi}4,\dfrac{9\pi}4,\dfrac{15\pi}4$, giving $2x=0,\dfrac\pi2,2\pi,\dfrac{5\pi}2,4\pi$ and $x=0,\dfrac\pi4,\pi,\dfrac{5\pi}4,2\pi$.

prev.question: Express $\cos2x+\sin2x$ in the form $R\cos(2x-\alpha)$, where $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$.
prev.answer: $R\cos(2x-\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\cos2x+R\sin\alpha\sin2x$, so $R\cos\alpha=1$ and $R\sin\alpha=1$. $R=\sqrt2$ and $\tan\alpha=1$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi4$. $\cos2x+\sin2x=\sqrt2\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi4\right)$.

questions.question: Let $u=\sqrt x$. Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^4\dfrac1{\sqrt x\left(1+\sqrt x\right)}dx$.
questions.answer: $x=u^2$, $dx=2u\,du$; $x=1\to u=1$ and $x=4\to u=2$. $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{2u}{u(1+u)}du=2\int_1^2\dfrac1{1+u}du=2\Big[\ln(1+u)\Big]_1^2=2(\ln3-\ln2)=2\ln\dfrac32\ \left(=\ln\dfrac94\right)$.

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac x{x+1}>3$.
questions.answer: Multiply by $(x+1)^2>0$ ($x\ne-1$): $x(x+1)>3(x+1)^2$, so $0>3(x+1)^2-x(x+1)=(x+1)(2x+3)$. This holds between the roots: $-\dfrac32<x<-1$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the angle between $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$. Give your answer in exact form.
questions.answer: $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=-2+10=8$, $|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{29}$, $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt5$. $\cos\theta=\dfrac8{\sqrt{145}}$, so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\dfrac8{\sqrt{145}}$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find $\lambda$, given that $\underset{\sim}{c}=\underset{\sim}{b}+\lambda\underset{\sim}{a}$ is perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a+\lambda|\mathbf a|^2=8+29\lambda=0$, so $\lambda=-\dfrac8{29}$.

prev.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the angle between $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$. Give your answer in exact form.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
questions.answer: Area $=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\dfrac8{\sqrt{145}}$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac9{\sqrt{145}}$ and area $=\sqrt{145}\cdot\dfrac9{\sqrt{145}}=9$ square units. (Alternatively, $|(-2)(2)-(5)(1)|=9$.)

questions.question: Prove that $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{1+2\cos^2\theta-1}=\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\tan\theta$.

questions.question: Use mathematical induction to prove that $7^n-1$ is divisible by 6 for all positive integers $n$.
questions.answer:
$n=1$: $7-1=6=6\times1$, true.

Assume $7^k-1=6M$ for some integer $M$. Then $7^{k+1}-1=7\cdot7^k-1=7(6M+1)-1=42M+6=6(7M+1)$, which is divisible by 6 since $7M+1$ is an integer. So true for $n=k+1$. By induction, true for all positive integers $n$.

questions.question: Let $O$, $A$ and $B$ be three points. Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$ and $AQ:QB=2:1$. Express $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ in terms of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf a+\dfrac13(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\dfrac23\mathbf a+\dfrac13\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\mathbf a+\dfrac23(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\mathbf b$.

questions.question: Let $O$, $A$ and $B$ be three points. Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$ and $AQ:QB=2:1$. Show that $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\dfrac13(\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a})$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\left(\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\mathbf b\right)-\left(\dfrac23\mathbf a+\dfrac13\mathbf b\right)=\dfrac13(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$.

questions.question: Let $O$, $A$ and $B$ be three points. Let $\underset{\sim}{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$ and $AQ:QB=2:1$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Use vectors to show that $\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{MQ}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$. $\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{OM}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)-\dfrac23\mathbf a-\dfrac13\mathbf b=\dfrac16(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. $\overrightarrow{MQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\mathbf b-\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=\dfrac16(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. Hence $\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{MQ}$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$.

questions.question: The coefficients of $x^2$ and $x^5$ are equal in the expansion of $(x+a)^8$. Find the value of the positive constant $a$.
questions.answer: The coefficient of $x^2$ is ${}^8C_6a^6=28a^6$ and of $x^5$ is ${}^8C_3a^3=56a^3$. $28a^6=56a^3$ gives $a^3(a^3-2)=0$, and since $a>0$, $a=\sqrt[3]2$.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}(3x)\right)$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}3x\right)=\tan^{-1}(3x)+\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}$.

questions.question: Hence find $\displaystyle\int\tan^{-1}(3x)\,dx$.
questions.answer: From part (i), $\tan^{-1}(3x)=\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}3x\right)-\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}$. $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}dx=\dfrac16\ln(1+9x^2)$ (since $\dfrac d{dx}(1+9x^2)=18x$). So $\displaystyle\int\tan^{-1}(3x)dx=x\tan^{-1}(3x)-\dfrac16\ln(1+9x^2)+C$.

prev.question: Find $\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}(3x)\right)$.
prev.answer: $\dfrac d{dx}\left(x\tan^{-1}3x\right)=\tan^{-1}(3x)+\dfrac{3x}{1+9x^2}$.

questions.question: The population, $P$, of porgs on the remote island of Ahch-To satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac12P\left(1-\dfrac P{2000}\right)$, where $t$ is the time in years. Initially there are 300 porgs. Find an expression for $P$ in terms of $t$. You may assume that $\dfrac{2000}{P(2000-P)}=\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{2000-P}$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(2000-P)}{4000}$, so $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{2000-P}\right)dP=\int\dfrac12dt$. $\ln|P|-\ln|2000-P|=\dfrac t2+C$, so $\dfrac P{2000-P}=Ae^{t/2}$ and $P=\dfrac{2000Ae^{t/2}}{1+Ae^{t/2}}=\dfrac{2000}{1+Be^{-t/2}}$, where $B=\dfrac1A$. $P(0)=300$: $1+B=\dfrac{20}3$, so $B=\dfrac{17}3$. $P=\dfrac{2000}{1+\frac{17}3e^{-t/2}}=\dfrac{6000}{3+17e^{-t/2}}$.

questions.question: The population, $P$, of porgs on the remote island of Ahch-To satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac12P\left(1-\dfrac P{2000}\right)$, where $t$ is the time in years. Initially there are 300 porgs. Find the greatest value of $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$. You do not need to justify that it is a maximum.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac P2-\dfrac{P^2}{4000}$ is a downward parabola in $P$ with vertex at $P=\dfrac{1/2}{2/4000}=1000$. The maximum value is $\dfrac12(1000)\left(1-\dfrac12\right)=250$ (people per year).

questions.question: The region bounded by $y=\cos x$, $y=\sin x$ and the $y$-axis is rotated about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the resulting solid.
questions.answer: $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(\cos^2x-\sin^2x\right)dx=\pi\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos2x\,dx=\pi\Big[\dfrac12\sin2x\Big]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac\pi2$ cubic units.

questions.question: In how many arrangements of the letters of the word TATOOINE are the Ts separated by one or more letters?
questions.answer: Total arrangements: $\dfrac{8!}{2!2!}=10080$. Arrangements with the Ts adjacent (treat TT as one object): $\dfrac{7!}{2!}=2520$. Ts separated: $10080-2520=7560$.

questions.question: The graph $y=P(x)$ of the quartic polynomial $P(x)=x^4-10x^3+bx^2+cx+16$ touches, but does not cross, the $x$-axis at two distinct points. Explain why $P(x)=(x-m)^2(x-n)^2$ for some real numbers $m$ and $n$.
questions.answer: The graph touches without crossing at an $x$-intercept, so each of the two intercepts is a zero of even multiplicity. A quartic has four zeroes counting multiplicity, so each of the two zeroes has multiplicity 2 and the leading coefficient is 1: $P(x)=(x-m)^2(x-n)^2$.

questions.question: The graph $y=P(x)$ of the quartic polynomial $P(x)=x^4-10x^3+bx^2+cx+16$ touches, but does not cross, the $x$-axis at two distinct points. Given that $mn<0$, find the possible values of $m$ and $n$.
questions.answer: $(x-m)^2(x-n)^2=x^4-2(m+n)x^3+\left(m^2+4mn+n^2\right)x^2-2mn(m+n)x+m^2n^2$. Comparing coefficients: $2(m+n)=10$ so $m+n=5$, and $m^2n^2=16$ so $mn=\pm4$. As $mn<0$, $mn=-4$. So $m,n$ are the roots of $t^2-5t-4=0$: $t=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{41}}2$. Hence $\{m,n\}=\left\{\dfrac{5+\sqrt{41}}2,\dfrac{5-\sqrt{41}}2\right\}$ (either way round).

prev.question: The graph $y=P(x)$ of the quartic polynomial $P(x)=x^4-10x^3+bx^2+cx+16$ touches, but does not cross, the $x$-axis at two distinct points. Explain why $P(x)=(x-m)^2(x-n)^2$ for some real numbers $m$ and $n$.
prev.answer: The graph touches without crossing at an $x$-intercept, so each of the two intercepts is a zero of even multiplicity. A quartic has four zeroes counting multiplicity, so each of the two zeroes has multiplicity 2 and the leading coefficient is 1: $P(x)=(x-m)^2(x-n)^2$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $y=u(x)\cos x$, where $u$ is some function of $x$, to solve the differential equation $y'\cos x=y\sin x+\cos x\sin x$.
questions.answer: $y'=u'\cos x-u\sin x$. Substituting: $(u'\cos x-u\sin x)\cos x=u\cos x\sin x+\cos x\sin x$. Dividing by $\cos x$: $u'\cos x-u\sin x=u\sin x+\sin x$, so $u'\cos x=(2u+1)\sin x$ and $u'=(2u+1)\tan x$. Separate variables: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{du}{2u+1}=\int\tan x\,dx$, so $\dfrac12\ln|2u+1|=-\ln|\cos x|+C$. Then $2u+1=A\sec^2x$ and $u=\dfrac{A\sec^2x-1}2$. Hence $y=u\cos x=\dfrac{A\sec x-\cos x}2$.

questions.question:
Shugo Maki hits a ball from a point 1 m above horizontal ground. The origin $O$ is the point on the ground directly below the point of projection. The ball passes directly over a fielder standing 85 m from the origin. A wall of height 5 m is 117.7 m from the origin. The ball is projected with speed $V$ m/s at an angle of elevation $\theta$. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The motion of the ball is modelled by $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\,t\\1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

On one occasion, Maki hits the ball with speed 34.3 m/s at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. At the instant the ball is hit, the fielder runs directly towards the wall at a constant speed of $W$ m/s. Assume that the fielder can catch the ball provided its height does not exceed 2 m. Find the minimum value of $W$ required for the fielder to catch the ball before the ball reaches the wall. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.answer:
Height $y=2$: $1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2=2$, so $5t^2-V\sin\theta\,t+1=0$. With $V\sin45^\circ=V\cos45^\circ=\dfrac{34.3}{\sqrt2}\approx24.254$, the later root (when the ball is descending through 2 m) is $t=\dfrac{24.254+\sqrt{24.254^2-20}}{10}\approx4.809$ s. At this time the ball is at $x=24.254\times4.809\approx116.64$ m, which is before the wall.

The fielder starts at 85 m, so he is at $85+Wt$. For the catch, $85+Wt=V\cos\theta\,t$, so $W=24.254-\dfrac{85}t$. This increases with $t$, so the minimum $W$ corresponds to the earliest time the ball is catchable, $t\approx4.809$: $W\approx24.254-\dfrac{85}{4.809}\approx6.58$ m/s.

questions.question: Shugo Maki hits a ball from a point 1 m above horizontal ground. The origin $O$ is the point on the ground directly below the point of projection. The ball passes directly over a fielder standing 85 m from the origin. A wall of height 5 m is 117.7 m from the origin. The ball is projected with speed $V$ m/s at an angle of elevation $\theta$. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The motion of the ball is modelled by $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\theta\,t\\1+V\sin\theta\,t-5t^2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) For a projected speed $V$ and angle of elevation $\theta$, show that the height of the ball when it reaches the wall is $y=1+117.7\tan\theta-\dfrac{5(117.7)^2}{V^2}\sec^2\theta$.
questions.answer: At the wall, $V\cos\theta\,t=117.7$, so $t=\dfrac{117.7}{V\cos\theta}$. Then $y=1+V\sin\theta\cdot\dfrac{117.7}{V\cos\theta}-5\cdot\dfrac{117.7^2}{V^2\cos^2\theta}=1+117.7\tan\theta-\dfrac{5(117.7)^2}{V^2}\sec^2\theta$.

questions.question: What is the solution to $|2x-5|>7$?

The projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is given by $\left(\dfrac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|^2}\right)\mathbf v$. What is the projection of $\mathbf u=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j$ onto $\mathbf v=-\mathbf i+2\mathbf j$?
questions.answer: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=-2+6=4$ and $|\mathbf v|^2=1+4=5$, so the projection is $\frac45(-\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)$ (C).

questions.question: Garrett, Dean, John L. and John T. sit at the kitchen bench in a row. In how many ways can the two Johns sit together?
questions.answer: Treat the two Johns as one block: $3!=6$ arrangements of the three “objects” (Garrett, Dean, block). Within the block the Johns can be ordered in $2!=2$ ways. Total $3!\times2!=12$ (A).

questions.question: Consider the integral $I=\displaystyle\int_0^3\frac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx$. The substitution $x=3\sin\theta$ is applied. Which of the following is obtained?
questions.answer: With $x=3\sin\theta$, $dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta$. Limits: $x=0\to\theta=0$, $x=3\to\theta=\frac\pi2$. $9-x^2=9-9\sin^2\theta=9\cos^2\theta$. So $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{3\cos\theta}{9\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta=\frac13\int_0^{\pi/2}\sec\theta\,d\theta$ (D).

questions.question: How many distinct solutions are there to the equation $\sin3x+\cos x=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$?
questions.answer: Write $\sin3x=-\cos x=\sin\left(x-\frac\pi2\right)$. Then either $3x=x-\frac\pi2+2k\pi$, giving $x=-\frac\pi4+k\pi$, i.e. $x=\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}4$ in the interval; or $3x=\pi-\left(x-\frac\pi2\right)+2k\pi=\frac{3\pi}2-x+2k\pi$, giving $x=\frac{3\pi}8+\frac{k\pi}2$, i.e. $x=\frac{3\pi}8,\frac{7\pi}8,\frac{11\pi}8,\frac{15\pi}8$. These six values are distinct, so there are 6 solutions (D). (Equivalently, the graphs of $y=\sin3x$ and $y=-\cos x$ meet 6 times.)

questions.question: Given that $A$ is a non-zero constant, which of the following integrals is equal to zero?
questions.answer: A definite integral over $[-A,A]$ is zero when the integrand is odd. $\sin x$, $\tan x$, $\sin^{-1}x$ and $\tan^{-1}x$ are odd, $\cos x$ is even, and $\cos^{-1}x$ is neither. Odd $\times$ even is odd: $\tan^{-1}(x)\cos(x)$ is odd, so the integral in C is $0$. (In A and D, $\cos^{-1}x\times$ odd is not odd, and in B, odd $\times$ odd is even.)

questions.question: Which of the following graphs could be a solution to the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+2y$?
questions.answer: Solving, $y=Ce^{2x}-\frac x2-\frac14$; for $C>0$ this decreases, reaches a minimum where $x+2y=0$, then rises steeply — the shape of graph A. The others are impossible: in B the maximum lies on the $y$-axis at positive $y$, but at $x=0$ the gradient is $2y\neq0$ there; in C the line passes through the origin but at the origin the gradient must be $0+2(0)=0$, whereas the line is steep; in D the curve has a horizontal asymptote, so $\frac{dy}{dx}\to0$, but $x+2y$ cannot tend to $0$ while $x\to\infty$ with $y$ bounded.

questions.question: Given that $x^3-4x^2+c\equiv(x-1)Q(x)+3$, where $Q(x)$ is a polynomial, what is the value of $c$?
questions.answer: Substitute $x=1$: $1-4+c=0+3$, so $c=6$ (D).

questions.question: The vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ have magnitudes of 4 and 7 respectively. Given that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}3$ and there exists a vector $\mathbf c$ such that $\mathbf a+\mathbf b=-\mathbf c$, what is the magnitude of $\mathbf c$ to the nearest whole number?
questions.answer: $|\mathbf c|^2=|\mathbf a+\mathbf b|^2=|\mathbf a|^2+|\mathbf b|^2+2\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=16+49+2(4)(7)\cos\frac{2\pi}3=65-28=37$. So $|\mathbf c|=\sqrt{37}\approx6.08$, which is 6 to the nearest whole number (B).

questions.question: Let $g(x)$ be the inverse function of $f(x)$. If we know that $f(2)=4$, $f(3)=2$, $f'(3)=-1$ and $f'(2)=-2$, what is the derivative of $g(x)$ when $x=2$?
questions.answer: Since $f(3)=2$, $g(2)=3$. The derivative of an inverse function is $g'(x)=\frac{1}{f'(g(x))}$, so $g'(2)=\frac{1}{f'(3)}=\frac1{-1}=-1$ (A).

questions.question: Find the inverse function of $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}$.
questions.answer: Let $y=\frac{x+1}{x-1}$ and swap $x$ and $y$: $x=\frac{y+1}{y-1}$. Then $xy-x=y+1$, so $y(x-1)=x+1$ and $y=\frac{x+1}{x-1}$. So $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}$ (the function is its own inverse).

questions.question: Solve $\cos2\theta+\cos\theta=1$ for $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$.
questions.answer: Use $\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$: $2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-2=0$. By the quadratic formula, $\cos\theta=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1+16}}{4}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{17}}{4}$. Since $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$, reject $\frac{-1-\sqrt{17}}4\approx-1.28$. So $\cos\theta=\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}4\approx0.781$, giving $\theta\approx0.675$ or $\theta=2\pi-0.675\approx5.608$ (3 decimal places).

questions.question: Sketch $y=3\sin^{-1}\dfrac x2$.
questions.answer: This is $y=\sin^{-1}x$ stretched horizontally by a factor of 2 and vertically by a factor of 3. The domain is $-2\le x\le2$ and the range is $-\frac{3\pi}2\le y\le\frac{3\pi}2$. The graph is odd, increasing, passes through the origin and has endpoints $\left(-2,-\frac{3\pi}2\right)$ and $\left(2,\frac{3\pi}2\right)$, with a vertical tangent at each endpoint (see graph).

questions.question: If $\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}m\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular, find the value of $m$.
questions.answer: Perpendicular vectors have $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0$: $2m+12=0$, so $m=-6$.

questions.question: The roots of $P(x)=2x^3-3x^2+x-6$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Find the value of $\alpha^2\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta^2\gamma+\alpha\beta\gamma^2$.
questions.answer: $\alpha^2\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta^2\gamma+\alpha\beta\gamma^2=\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$. For $2x^3-3x^2+x-6$: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac32$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma=-\frac{-6}{2}=3$. So the value is $3\times\frac32=\dfrac92$.

questions.question: The roots of $P(x)=2x^3-3x^2+x-6$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.
questions.answer: $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)$. Here $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac32$ and $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\frac12$. So the value is $\left(\frac32\right)^2-2\left(\frac12\right)=\frac94-1=\dfrac54$.

questions.question: If $\sin x=\dfrac35$, where $x$ is acute, find the exact value of $\cos2x$.
questions.answer: $\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x=1-2\left(\frac35\right)^2=1-\frac{18}{25}=\dfrac7{25}$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\sin^22x\,dx$.
questions.answer: Use $\cos4x=1-2\sin^22x$, so $\sin^22x=\frac12(1-\cos4x)$. Then $\int\sin^22x\,dx=\frac12\int(1-\cos4x)\,dx=\frac12\left(x-\frac{\sin4x}4\right)+C=\dfrac x2-\dfrac{\sin4x}8+C$.

questions.question: By expressing $2\cos\theta-\sqrt5\sin\theta$ in terms of $R\cos(\theta+\alpha)$, where $R>0$ and $0\le\alpha\le\frac\pi2$, solve $2\cos\theta=\sqrt5\sin\theta-3$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
questions.answer: $R\cos(\theta+\alpha)=R\cos\theta\cos\alpha-R\sin\theta\sin\alpha$, so $R\cos\alpha=2$ and $R\sin\alpha=\sqrt5$. Then $R^2=4+5=9$, $R=3$, and $\tan\alpha=\frac{\sqrt5}2$, so $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt5}2$ (acute). The equation becomes $2\cos\theta-\sqrt5\sin\theta=-3$, i.e. $3\cos(\theta+\alpha)=-3$, so $\cos(\theta+\alpha)=-1$. For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$ we have $\alpha\le\theta+\alpha\le2\pi+\alpha$ with $\alpha<\frac\pi2$, so the only solution is $\theta+\alpha=\pi$, giving $\theta=\pi-\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt5}2\ (\approx2.30)$.

questions.question: Solve the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy-x$, given $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-3$ when $x=-3$.
questions.answer: When $x=-3$, $\frac{dy}{dx}=-3$: $-3=-3y+3$, so $y=2$. Now $\frac{dy}{dx}=x(y-1)$, so $\int\frac{dy}{y-1}=\int x\,dx$, giving $\ln|y-1|=\frac{x^2}2+C$. Substituting $x=-3$, $y=2$: $\ln1=\frac92+C$, so $C=-\frac92$. Hence $\ln|y-1|=\frac{x^2}2-\frac92$, so $y-1=e^{(x^2-9)/2}$ (positive, since $y-1=1>0$ at the given point), i.e. $y=1+e^{\frac{x^2-9}{2}}$.

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac{x}{3x+1}\ge1$.
questions.answer: Note $x\neq-\frac13$. Multiply both sides by $(3x+1)^2>0$: $x(3x+1)\ge(3x+1)^2$, so $0\ge(3x+1)^2-x(3x+1)=(3x+1)(2x+1)$. The product $(3x+1)(2x+1)\le0$ between its roots $-\frac12$ and $-\frac13$. Since $x\ne-\frac13$: $-\dfrac12\le x<-\dfrac13$.

questions.question: Consider the region between the $x$-axis, $y$-axis, the line $y=10$ and the function $y=-\dfrac{1}{0.7}\ln\dfrac{x-1}{3}$, as shown in the diagram. When the region is rotated about the $y$-axis, it forms the volume of the bell of Hannah’s clarinet. Find the volume of the bell.
questions.answer: Rotating about the $y$-axis, $V=\pi\int_0^{10}x^2\,dy$. From $y=-\frac1{0.7}\ln\frac{x-1}3$: $-0.7y=\ln\frac{x-1}{3}$, so $x=1+3e^{-0.7y}$. Then $x^2=1+6e^{-0.7y}+9e^{-1.4y}$ and $V=\pi\int_0^{10}\left(1+6e^{-0.7y}+9e^{-1.4y}\right)dy=\pi\left[y-\frac{6}{0.7}e^{-0.7y}-\frac9{1.4}e^{-1.4y}\right]_0^{10}=\pi\left[10-\frac{60}7e^{-7}-\frac{45}7e^{-14}+\frac{60}7+\frac{45}7\right]=\pi\left[25-\frac{60}7e^{-7}-\frac{45}7e^{-14}\right]$ cubic units ($\approx78.5$).

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int_0^2\frac{x}{x^4+16}\,dx$ using the substitution $u=x^2$.
questions.answer: $u=x^2$, $du=2x\,dx$ so $x\,dx=\frac12du$; limits $x=0\to u=0$, $x=2\to u=4$. $\int_0^2\frac{x}{x^4+16}dx=\frac12\int_0^4\frac{du}{u^2+16}=\frac12\left[\frac14\tan^{-1}\frac u4\right]_0^4=\frac18\left(\tan^{-1}1-\tan^{-1}0\right)=\dfrac\pi{32}$.

questions.question: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{2y-2}$ and $y=1$ when $x=0$, find $y$ as a function of $x$.
questions.answer: Separate variables: $\int(2y-2)\,dy=\int3\,dx$, so $y^2-2y=3x+C$. When $x=0$, $y=1$: $1-2=C$, so $C=-1$. Then $y^2-2y+1=3x$, i.e. $(y-1)^2=3x$, so $y=1\pm\sqrt{3x}$ (for $x\ge0$). Both branches satisfy the differential equation and the condition $y=1$ at $x=0$, so the solution is $y=1\pm\sqrt{3x}$.

questions.question:
Briar Hawks is the men’s varsity ice hockey team at Briar University. The team has 12 players that make up **four** forward lines (3 players each) and 6 players that make up the **three** defensive lines (2 players each). The forward and defensive lines rotate time on the ice during the game. (Note defensive players and offensive players never swap roles.)

In how many ways can the three defensive lines be made?
questions.answer: Choose the pairs for the lines in turn: $\binom62\binom42\binom22=15\times6\times1=90$. The three lines are indistinguishable (just three equal groups of 2), so divide by $3!$: $\dfrac{90}{3!}=15$ ways.

questions.question:
Briar Hawks is the men’s varsity ice hockey team at Briar University. The team has 12 players that make up **four** forward lines (3 players each) and 6 players that make up the **three** defensive lines (2 players each). The forward and defensive lines rotate time on the ice during the game. (Note defensive players and offensive players never swap roles.)

How many player combinations are possible on the ice (3 forwards and 2 defenders at a time)?
questions.answer: Choose the 3 forwards from the 12 forwards: $\binom{12}3=220$. Choose the 2 defenders from the 6 defenders: $\binom62=15$. By the multiplication principle there are $220\times15=3300$ possible combinations.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction that the sum of the squares of the first $2n$ positive integers can be given by $1^2+2^2+3^2+\cdots+(2n)^2=\dfrac{n(2n+1)(4n+1)}3$.
questions.answer: **Base case** $n=1$: LHS $=1^2+2^2=5$; RHS $=\frac{1(3)(5)}3=5$ ✓. **Assume** true for $n=k$: $1^2+\dots+(2k)^2=\frac{k(2k+1)(4k+1)}3$. **Prove** for $n=k+1$: $1^2+\dots+(2k+2)^2=\frac{(k+1)(2k+3)(4k+5)}3$. LHS $=\left[1^2+\dots+(2k)^2\right]+(2k+1)^2+(2k+2)^2=\frac{k(2k+1)(4k+1)}3+(2k+1)^2+(2k+2)^2=\frac{8k^3+6k^2+k+3(4k^2+4k+1)+3(4k^2+8k+4)}3=\frac{8k^3+30k^2+37k+15}3$. RHS $=\frac{(k+1)(2k+3)(4k+5)}3=\frac{(k+1)(8k^2+22k+15)}3=\frac{8k^3+30k^2+37k+15}3$ ✓. So true for $n=k+1$ whenever true for $n=k$; being true for $n=1$, it is true for all positive integers $n$ by induction.

questions.question: An ice hockey player, who is 200 cm tall with ice skates on, skates from directly under a single overhead light mounted at a height of 10 m from the ice. He skates at a constant rate of $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ away from the light towards the edge of the rink which is 30 m from his starting point. When the ice hockey player is $x$ m from his starting point, is the ice hockey player or the tip of his shadow moving more rapidly? Justify your solution with calculations. (Let $y$ m be the distance of the tip of his shadow from the point under the light.)
questions.answer: By similar triangles (light at height 10 m, player 2 m tall): $\frac{y}{10}=\frac{y-x}{2}$, so $2y=10y-10x$ and $y=\frac54x$. The player moves at $\frac{dx}{dt}=3$ m/s, so the tip of the shadow moves at $\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac54\times3=3.75$ m/s. This is greater than $3$ m/s, so the **tip of his shadow** moves more rapidly (at every position $x$).

questions.question: The diagram shows two triangles $OAB$ and $BCD$. The point $M$ is the point of intersection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD}$. The point $C$ lies on $\overrightarrow{OB}$ such that $\overrightarrow{OB}=4\overrightarrow{OC}$. $\overrightarrow{OA}$ is parallel to $\overrightarrow{BD}$ (in the same direction) and $|\overrightarrow{OA}|=2|\overrightarrow{BD}|$. Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$. Find $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{CM}|}{|\overrightarrow{CD}|}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{OC}=\frac14\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}=\frac12\mathbf a$. $\overrightarrow{CD}=\overrightarrow{CB}+\overrightarrow{BD}=\frac34\mathbf b+\frac12\mathbf a$. Since $M$ is on $CD$, let $\overrightarrow{CM}=\lambda\overrightarrow{CD}$ (so the required ratio is $\lambda$): $\overrightarrow{CM}=\frac\lambda2\mathbf a+\frac{3\lambda}4\mathbf b$. Since $M$ is on $AB$, let $\overrightarrow{AM}=\mu\overrightarrow{AB}=\mu(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$. Then $\overrightarrow{CM}=\overrightarrow{CO}+\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AM}=-\frac14\mathbf b+\mathbf a+\mu\mathbf b-\mu\mathbf a=(1-\mu)\mathbf a+\left(\mu-\frac14\right)\mathbf b$. As $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are not parallel, equate coefficients: $\frac\lambda2=1-\mu$ and $\frac{3\lambda}4=\mu-\frac14$. Adding: $\frac{5\lambda}4=\frac34$, so $\lambda=\frac35$. Therefore $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{CM}|}{|\overrightarrow{CD}|}=\dfrac35$.

questions.question: By considering $(1+x)^{1000}+(1+x)^{999}+(1+x)^{998}+\cdots+(1+x)^{950}$, or otherwise, show that $\dbinom{1000}{50}+\dbinom{999}{49}+\dbinom{998}{48}+\cdots+\dbinom{950}{0}=\dbinom{1001}{50}$.
questions.answer: The sum $S=(1+x)^{950}\left[1+(1+x)+\dots+(1+x)^{50}\right]$ is a geometric series with 51 terms, ratio $(1+x)$: $S=(1+x)^{950}\cdot\frac{(1+x)^{51}-1}{(1+x)-1}=\frac{(1+x)^{1001}-(1+x)^{950}}{x}$. Compare the coefficients of $x^{950}$. On the left (original form), the coefficient of $x^{950}$ in $(1+x)^k$ is $\binom{k}{950}$, so it is $\binom{1000}{950}+\binom{999}{950}+\dots+\binom{950}{950}$. On the right, the coefficient of $x^{950}$ in $\frac{(1+x)^{1001}}{x}$ is the coefficient of $x^{951}$ in $(1+x)^{1001}$, namely $\binom{1001}{951}$, and $(1+x)^{950}$ has no $x^{951}$ term (so it contributes nothing to the coefficient of $x^{950}$ after dividing by $x$). Hence $\binom{1000}{950}+\binom{999}{950}+\dots+\binom{950}{950}=\binom{1001}{951}$. Using $\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$: $\binom{1000}{950}=\binom{1000}{50}$, $\binom{999}{950}=\binom{999}{49}$, $\binom{998}{950}=\binom{998}{48}$, …, $\binom{950}{950}=\binom{950}0$, and $\binom{1001}{951}=\binom{1001}{50}$. So $\binom{1000}{50}+\binom{999}{49}+\dots+\binom{950}0=\binom{1001}{50}$.

questions.question: The equation $ax^3+cx+d=0$ has a double root. Show that $27ad^2+4c^3=0$.
questions.answer: Let the roots be $\alpha,\alpha,\beta$. Sum of roots (no $x^2$ term): $2\alpha+\beta=0$, so $\beta=-2\alpha$. Sum of products in pairs: $\alpha^2+2\alpha\beta=\frac ca$, i.e. $\alpha^2-4\alpha^2=-3\alpha^2=\frac ca$, so $\alpha^2=-\frac{c}{3a}$. Product of roots: $\alpha^2\beta=-\frac da$, i.e. $-2\alpha^3=-\frac da$, so $\alpha^3=\frac{d}{2a}$. Then $\left(\alpha^2\right)^3=\left(\alpha^3\right)^2$ gives $-\frac{c^3}{27a^3}=\frac{d^2}{4a^2}$. Multiply by $108a^3$: $-4c^3=27ad^2$, so $27ad^2+4c^3=0$.

questions.question: The equation $ax^3+cx+d=0$ has a double root precisely when $27ad^2+4c^3=0$. Hence, and without the use of calculus methods, find the exact values of the $y$-coordinates of the two stationary points on the curve $y=3x^3-4x+1$.
questions.answer: At a stationary point of $y=3x^3-4x+1$ with $y=m$, the equation $3x^3-4x+1-m=0$ has a double root (the horizontal line $y=m$ is tangent to the curve). So with $a=3$, $c=-4$, $d=1-m$: $27(3)(1-m)^2+4(-4)^3=0$, so $81(1-m)^2=256$ and $(1-m)^2=\frac{256}{81}$, $1-m=\pm\frac{16}9$. Hence $m=1\mp\frac{16}9$, i.e. $m=-\frac79$ or $m=\frac{25}9$. The $y$-coordinates of the stationary points are $\dfrac{25}9$ and $-\dfrac79$.

questions.question: Let $\mathbf x$, $\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf z$ be non-zero vectors. Let $\alpha$ be the angle between $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ and $\beta$ be the angle between $\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf z$, where $\alpha+\beta\neq\frac\pi2$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$. The angle between $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf z$ is $\alpha+\beta$ ($\mathbf x,\mathbf y,\mathbf z$ lie in a plane with $\mathbf y$ between $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf z$). If $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf y}\mathbf x=\mathbf u$, show that $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}\mathbf u=\dfrac{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos(\alpha+\beta)}\times\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}\mathbf x$.
questions.answer: Use $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf b}\mathbf a=\frac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf b|^2}\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta$. $\mathbf u=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf y}\mathbf x=\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y}{|\mathbf y|^2}\mathbf y$ with $\cos\alpha=\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y}{|\mathbf x||\mathbf y|}$; similarly $\cos\beta=\frac{\mathbf y\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf y||\mathbf z|}$ and $\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf x||\mathbf z|}$. Then $\text{RHS}=\frac{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos(\alpha+\beta)}\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}\mathbf x=\frac{\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y}{|\mathbf x||\mathbf y|}\cdot\frac{\mathbf y\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf y||\mathbf z|}}{\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf x||\mathbf z|}}\cdot\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf z|^2}\mathbf z=\frac{(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y)(\mathbf y\cdot\mathbf z)}{|\mathbf y|^2}\cdot\frac{\mathbf z}{|\mathbf z|^2}$. And LHS: $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf z|^2}\mathbf z=\frac{\left(\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y}{|\mathbf y|^2}\mathbf y\right)\cdot\mathbf z}{|\mathbf z|^2}\mathbf z=\frac{(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y)(\mathbf y\cdot\mathbf z)}{|\mathbf y|^2}\cdot\frac{\mathbf z}{|\mathbf z|^2}$. These are equal, so $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}\mathbf u=\frac{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos(\alpha+\beta)}\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}\mathbf x$ as required.

questions.question: A stone is projected from a point on the ground with speed $v$ m/s at angle $\theta$ and just clears a fence $h$ metres high, $d$ metres away. Air resistance is negligible and $x=vt\cos\theta$, $y=-\dfrac12gt^2+vt\sin\theta$. Show that $v^2=\dfrac{gd^2\sec^2\theta}{2(d\tan\theta-h)}$.
questions.answer:
Eliminating $t=\dfrac{x}{v\cos\theta}$: $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{gx^2\sec^2\theta}{2v^2}$. At $x=d$, $y=h$:

$$\frac{gd^2\sec^2\theta}{2v^2}=d\tan\theta-h\implies v^2=\frac{gd^2\sec^2\theta}{2(d\tan\theta-h)}$$

questions.question: A stone is projected from a point on the ground with speed $v$ m/s at angle $\theta$ and just clears a fence $h$ metres high, $d$ metres away. Air resistance is negligible and $x=vt\cos\theta$, $y=-\dfrac12gt^2+vt\sin\theta$. Given $v^2=\dfrac{gd^2\sec^2\theta}{2(d\tan\theta-h)}$, show that the maximum height reached is $\dfrac{d^2\tan^2\theta}{4(d\tan\theta-h)}$.
questions.answer:
$\dot y=0$ when $t=\dfrac{v\sin\theta}g$, giving $y_{\max}=\dfrac{v^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$. Substituting for $v^2$:

$$y_{\max}=\frac{d^2\sec^2\theta\sin^2\theta}{4(d\tan\theta-h)}=\frac{d^2\tan^2\theta}{4(d\tan\theta-h)}$$

questions.question: A stone is projected from a point on the ground with speed $v$ m/s at angle $\theta$ and just clears a fence $h$ metres high, $d$ metres away. Air resistance is negligible and $x=vt\cos\theta$, $y=-\dfrac12gt^2+vt\sin\theta$. Given that the maximum height is $\dfrac{d^2\tan^2\theta}{4(d\tan\theta-h)}$, show that the stone, when at its maximum height, will just clear the fence if $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2h}d$.
questions.answer:
Set the maximum height equal to $h$: $d^2\tan^2\theta=4h(d\tan\theta-h)$, so

$$d^2\tan^2\theta-4hd\tan\theta+4h^2=(d\tan\theta-2h)^2=0$$

Hence $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2h}d$.
